newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish '97 inflation forecast at 1.8pct - Central Bank.
newsitem.headline: Irish '97 inflation forecast at 1.8pct - Central Bank.

text.p: Ireland's Central Bank on Tuesday forecast Irish inflation at 1.8 percent and expected real GNP to increase by a further 5.75 percent in 1997.
"Inflation this year is expected to be around 1.8 percent, reflecting, in significant part, the benefits of the firm exchange rate in 1996," the central bank said in its annual report.
It said inflation was, however, expected to be on an upward trend over the remainder of 1997 and into 1998.

The central bank said the inflation forecast depended on the "evolution of the exchange rate" during most of 1997 adding that monetary policy will continue to focus on price stability as the priority.

It said on the domestic front, both house prices and credit continue to grow strongly and while the current inflation performance was satisfactory there "are pressures that point to a rise in inflation in the second half of the year".
"Against this background, the continuation of moderate wage increases in both public and private sectors is the best assurance of strong employment growth in the years ahead," it said.
The central bank forecast real growth in personal consumer expenditure of about 5.0 percent in 1997 and expected investment expenditure to rise by 7.25 percent, down from 9.0 percent in 1996.
The central bank said growth in Ireland's main trading partners was expected to accelerate to about 2.6 percent in 1997.
"With the pick-up in continental European markets, merchandise export volumes are forecast to increase by 8.5 percent, up from 8.75 percent in 1996," it said.
It expected merchandise import growth to increase by 8.5 percent due to continued strong domestic growth.
The central bank said the overall surplus on the current account of the balance of payments is expected to be about 5.5 percent in 1997 - broadly similar to 1996.
On the exchange rate front the Central Bank reported "substantial negative foreign-exchange market intervention" in April when the Irish pound came under pressure.
The pressure stemmed from market focus on the possibility that the currency might move closer to its ERM central rate, it said.

The bank said it intervened in both directions in the first quarter to smooth movements of the currency. In January sizeable net positive interventions were recorded but in February and March postive and negative interventions broadly offset each other, it said.
In April there was a net negative foreign exchange intervention of about 1.2 billion pounds, the bank added.
